XXI. Acceptance, Notice of Breach & § 2-714 Damages — §§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717 WEEK 9

RULE Acceptance, § 2-606(1): buyer accepts when, after a reasonable opportunity to inspect, it (a) signifies the goods conform or that it will keep them despite nonconformity; (b) fails to make an effective rejection; or (c) does any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership.

Effect of acceptance | Rule
Owes the price | § 2-607(1)
Must notify of breach within a reasonable time or be barred from any remedy | § 2-607(3)(a)
Bears the burden of proving breach | § 2-607(4). (After rejection, the burden falls on whichever party sues.)
Loses the right to reject | § 2-607(2)
Loses the right to cancel, and cover or market damages | Unless buyer revokes. An installment contract may differ: §§ 2-612(3), 2-711(1)
Gains value-difference damages + incidental and consequential | §§ 2-714, 2-715

- Losing the right to reject means buyer can't force goods back on the seller to escape a falling market.

Notice of breach

- Purposes (Aqualon v. MAC Equipment (4th Cir. 1998), quoted p. 301): (1) prevent surprise and let the seller recommend how to fix the problem; (2) let the seller investigate and prepare; (3) open the way to settlement; (4) protect against stale claims. Also lets the seller preserve rights against its own supplier (Hebron v. American Isuzu).

- Because losing all remedies is draconian, courts are lenient, but many hold that some pre-suit notice is required; filing a complaint generally isn't enough. Reasonable time is a fact question (§§ 1-205, 1-202; Golden v. Den-Mat). Content: see § 2-607 cmt. 4.

- Don't confuse: § 2-605 applies to rejected goods; § 2-607(3)(a) applies to accepted goods.

- The parties may fix a reasonable time (§§ 1-205(b), 1-302). Whether they could dispense with notice altogether is an open question in the text.

Damages for accepted goods
RULE § 2-714: (1) for any nonconforming tender (e.g., late or short), the loss resulting in the ordinary course of events, determined in any reasonable manner. (2) For breach of warranty, value as warranted − value as accepted, at the time and place of acceptance, unless special circumstances show proximate damages of a different amount. (3) Incidental and consequential damages in a proper case.

RULE Deducting from the price, § 2-717: on notifying the seller, buyer may deduct all or part of its damages from any price still due under the same contract.

- Contract price plays no part in the § 2-714(2) formula. A buyer that struck a bad bargain keeps its bad bargain, and one that struck a good bargain keeps that too.

- Repair cost is a common proxy for value difference, not the statutory test. The text asks whether cost of repair or cost of replacement better measures the lost expectancy. Where repair costs more than the drop in value, the seller argues for the smaller figure; if repair leaves the goods worth less, the buyer adds the leftover loss.

- Consequential damages carry the same four limits as in Section XVIII and can far exceed the price.

XXIII. Privity & Remote Sellers — § 2-318 WEEK 10

- A contract claim normally needs privity. Vertical privity: a buyer in the chain of title suing a seller further up the chain (consumer vs. manufacturer). Horizontal privity: a non-buyer outside the chain, injured by the goods. Vertical privity exists only between immediate links; a buyer who didn't buy directly from a seller is "remote."

- First ask whether the remote seller made any warranty to this buyer. Express warranty under § 2-313? Implied warranty under § 2-314? Or a warranty to the distributor or retailer that extends to the buyer?

- Article 2 barely addresses privity. § 2-318 offers three alternatives, and comment 3 leaves room for case law on the distributive chain.

§ 2-318 | Who is protected | Injury covered | Vertical privity
Alt. A (majority) | Natural persons in buyer's family or household, or guests in buyer's home | Injury in person | Silent; left to case law
Alt. B | Any natural person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected | Injury in person | Implicitly abolished
Alt. C | Any person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected | "Injured": some states include property or economic loss | Eliminated

- A seller can't exclude § 2-318's reach, but disclaimers and remedy limits that bind the buyer bind beneficiaries too (§ 2-318 cmt. 1). Section VI has the overview of § 2-318.

MAIN CASE Hyundai Motor America, Inc. v. Goodin (Ind. 2005) — no vertical privity for a consumer's implied warranty claim Source: principal case, casebook pp. 328–337. No class slides. Facts: Sandra Goodin bought a new Hyundai Sonata from a dealer, with a 5-year/60,000-mile manufacturer warranty. Brake trouble began almost at once, and eight months of repairs didn't fix it. Her lawyer sought a refund; she sued Hyundai under the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act. The jury found for Hyundai on express warranty but for Goodin on the implied warranty of merchantability, awarding $3,000. The Court of Appeals reversed for lack of privity, feeling bound by a footnote in Martin Rispens. Held: Indiana doesn't require vertical privity between a consumer and a manufacturer for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability, even for economic loss. The footnote was dicta. Alternative A speaks only to horizontal privity and leaves vertical privity to the courts. Privity's freedom-of-contract rationale has "eroded to the point of invisibility" for many consumer goods: goods reach consumers through intermediaries; warranties are marketing tools; consumers expect merchantability; the law spreads the cost of lemons across all buyers; and a disclaimer in the dealer's buyer's order would otherwise leave her without a remedy. The privity bar began as a limit on tort claims (Winterbottom) and was undercut by MacPherson and Henningsen. Why it matters: The modern consumer rule, but courts remain divided. Limits: it speaks to a consumer against a manufacturer, for goods subject to Magnuson-Moss. Damages are usually the § 2-714(2) value difference.

After Goodin

- Express warranty: even privity states may not require it. A manufacturer shouldn't escape its public claims because the buyer bought through a dealer (p. 337).

- Open questions when privity falls away (pp. 338–339): Can a remote buyer reject or revoke and get a refund from the manufacturer, and of which price? May it recover § 2-712 or § 2-713 damages? Must notice go to the manufacturer, or is notice to the retailer enough? Are consequential damages tested by what the manufacturer or the retailer knew? When does the limitations period start? Which state's law applies when only one has abolished privity? Does a distributor owe the same duty?

- Only sellers make implied warranties. "Seller" = one who sells or contracts to sell (§ 2-103(1)(d)), and a sale passes title (§ 2-106(1)). Auctioneers, brokers, and other agents without title almost always aren't sellers.

- Amazon: for third-party vendors' goods, courts have held Amazon isn't a seller and makes no warranty, despite listing, payment processing, storage, and shipping. The § 2-403(2) entrustment argument fails for three reasons: Amazon may never possess the goods, and the vendor's identity is disclosed; an entrustee isn't necessarily "the seller"; and Amazon's terms disclaim implied warranties anyway.

XXIV. Seller's Remedies: Roadmap & When the Buyer Has the Goods — §§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702 WEEK 11

- Buyer's basic duties: accept and pay in accordance with the contract (§ 2-301).

- Walk the facts in order. Was the seller's refusal to tender justified (buyer failed to pay first, or to answer a proper demand for assurance)? Or was it a breach? Or does neither party breach, e.g., goods destroyed without fault? Is the buyer's breach excused? Are the seller's remedies limited?

- § 2-703 is an incomplete catalog. It has no "and" or "or," so it doesn't say which remedies combine (cmt. 1). The answer comes from § 1-305: no overcompensation. As with the buyer, the remedies depend on the nature of the breach and who has the goods.

Situation | Seller's remedy | Cite
Buyer accepted and won't pay | The price + incidental damages. Buyer may offset for nonconformity (§§ 2-714, 2-717) | §§ 2-709, 2-607(1)
Buyer has goods; payment device fails; or buyer took goods on credit while insolvent | Limited reclamation | §§ 2-507, 2-702(2)
Seller has the goods or they are in transit: repudiation, failure to pay before delivery, wrongful rejection, refused cure, wrongful revocation | Withhold or stop delivery; cancel; resale, market, or lost-profit damages; rarely the price | §§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705, 2-706, 2-708, 2-709
Any of these | Incidental damages, not consequential | §§ 2-710, 1-305(a)

RULE Action for the price, § 2-709(1): when buyer fails to pay the price as it becomes due, seller may recover the price, with incidental damages, of (a) goods accepted, or conforming goods lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time after risk of loss passed to buyer; and (b) goods identified to the contract if seller is unable after reasonable effort to resell them at a reasonable price, or circumstances reasonably indicate that effort would be unavailing.

- "Commercially reasonable time" limits only the lost-or-damaged goods, not accepted goods (p. 399 n.1).

- Worked example (p. 400): custom sign, $6,400; accepted; color wrong; buyer spends $1,300 reprinting brochures to match. Buyer owes $6,400, less any § 2-714 value difference and, if recoverable under § 2-715, the $1,300, deducted under § 2-717.

Getting goods back from a buyer that won't pay

- The general rule surprises people: an unpaid seller doesn't get the goods back. The principal right is the price, which is only as good as the buyer's ability to pay. Two exceptions:

- (1) Article 9 security interest. The seller who takes one may repossess peaceably or by replevin on default (§ 9-609). One sentence creates it: "seller retains a security interest in the goods sold to secure the buyer's obligations under this agreement." A clause that seller "retains title" does the same thing and no more, because title passes on delivery and the reservation is limited to a security interest (§§ 1-201(b)(35), 2-401(1), 9-109(a)(5)).

- (2) Reclamation. A restitutionary remedy, not an expectancy measure. Not self-help: if buyer doesn't return the goods voluntarily, seller must go to court.

| § 2-507 (failed payment) | § 2-702(2) (credit sale to an insolvent)
When | Cash sale: payment due on delivery; payment device fails, e.g., a check bounces. A check at delivery counts (§ 2-511 cmts. 4–6). A credit sale or post-dated check does not | Seller sold on credit and discovers buyer received the goods while insolvent (§ 1-201(b)(23))

Subject to | Rights of good faith purchasers, covered in Chapter 10 (not assigned) | Buyers in ordinary course and good faith purchasers (§ 2-702(3))

- Why the § 2-702(3) bar? Possibly reclamation rests on a rescission for fraud, so no expectancy remains; and the insolvent buyer's other creditors shouldn't be pushed further behind.

- Practice point: a seller on credit should take a security interest; reclamation is too narrow to rely on.

- Problem 9-1 (4,000 gallons of milk, into a vat with 5,000 others; half the vat becomes ice cream; demand June 7 for June 1 delivery): demand is within 10 days and the sale was on credit, so § 2-702(2) applies. Nothing for the ice cream, which is no longer the goods sold. The casebook cites Wheeling-Pittsburgh and Charter and gives no answer; the result is worked from the statute.

XXV. When the Seller Has the Goods: Withhold, Stop, Cancel — §§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705, 2-612 WEEK 11

- Withhold = seller has the goods. Stop = a carrier or other bailee has them.

RULE Withholding: seller may withhold delivery if buyer (1) wrongfully rejects, (2) wrongfully revokes, (3) fails to make a payment due, or (4) repudiates (§ 2-703(a)). If seller discovers buyer is insolvent, it may refuse delivery except for cash, including payment for all goods already delivered under the contract (§ 2-702(1)).

RULE Stopping in transit, § 2-705(1): seller may stop delivery in a carrier's or bailee's possession when it discovers buyer's insolvency (any size of shipment). For repudiation, failure to make a payment due before delivery, or any other right to withhold or reclaim, it may stop only carload, truckload, planeload, or larger shipments. § 2-705(2): the right ends on buyer's receipt; a bailee's (non-carrier) acknowledgment to buyer that it holds for buyer; a carrier's such acknowledgment by reshipment or as a warehouse; or negotiation to buyer of a negotiable document of title.

- Three questions: (1) does seller have the right as against buyer? (2) must the carrier obey? (3) who is liable if the carrier obeys or disobeys?

- Carrier, § 2-705(3): seller must give notice enabling the carrier, by reasonable diligence, to prevent delivery. The carrier must then hold and deliver as seller directs, and seller is liable for ensuing charges or damages. If a negotiable document was issued, the carrier need not obey until the document is surrendered. A carrier with a nonnegotiable bill need not obey a stop order from anyone but the consignor.

- Stopping is limited because of the burden on carriers (cmt. 1). Related: shipping under reservation (§ 2-505), which in effect gives seller a security interest and lets it withhold the goods until paid.

RULE Cancellation, § 2-703(f): in a non-installment contract, seller may cancel on any buyer breach. No notice is required. Cancellation ends future performance and doesn't waive damages (§ 2-106(4)). Installment contracts: seller may cancel the whole only if the breach substantially impairs the value of the whole contract (§§ 2-612(3), 2-703). Short of that it may demand assurance and suspend (§ 2-609; § 2-612 cmt. 6).

XXVI. Seller's Damages — §§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708, 2-709, 2-710 WEEK 11

- Four alternatives, all protecting the expectancy (§ 1-305), all with incidental damages: resale, market, lost profit, price. Seller can't stack resale and market.

- Worked example (pp. 408–410): $10,000 lithograph, buyer defaults. Worth $9,000: resell and get $1,000 (§ 2-706), or keep it and get $1,000 (§ 2-708(1)). Worth $11,000 or $10,000: no resale or market damages. Unlimited supply: the resale isn't a substitute, because Dealer would have made both sales, so its loss is the profit on one extra sale (§ 2-708(2)). Nobody else wants it: the price (§ 2-709), and buyer gets the print.

- Market damages are the more traditional remedy: they resemble the seller reselling to itself at market (n.11).

Measure | Formula | Key conditions | Plus / less
Resale § 2-706 | Contract − resale | Good faith; commercially reasonable in every aspect; notice | + incidental − saved
Market § 2-708(1) | Contract − market at time and place for tender | Proof of market price (§§ 2-723, 2-724) | + incidental − saved
Lost profit § 2-708(2) | Profit (including reasonable overhead) + costs reasonably incurred | § 2-708(1) inadequate; typically lost-volume sellers | + incidental
Price § 2-709 | Contract price | Accepted, or lost after risk passed, or can't be resold at a reasonable price | + incidental; hold goods for buyer

Resale — § 2-706
RULE § 2-706: where resale is in good faith and commercially reasonable, seller may recover contract price − resale price, + incidental damages, − expenses saved. Every aspect (method, manner, time, place, terms) must be commercially reasonable, and the resale must be reasonably identified as referring to the broken contract. Private sale: reasonable notification to buyer of the intent to resell (§ 2-706(3)). Public sale (auction): (1) only identified goods unless there is a recognized futures market; (2) at a usual place if available; (3) reasonable notice of time and place, except perishables; (4) goods available for inspection if not in view; (5) seller may buy.

- Resale isn't required. Seller resells because market price may be hard to prove and the resale price is known, and because sellers rarely want the goods.

- A bad resale doesn't cost seller its claim. It only loses this measure and falls back on § 2-708 (§ 2-706 cmt. 2).

- Good-faith purchaser takes free of the original buyer, even if seller botched the requirements (§ 2-706(5)). Seller keeps any profit on resale (§ 2-706(6)).

- Unidentified goods: the goods need not exist or be identified at breach (§ 2-706(2)), and § 2-704(1) lets seller identify conforming goods in its possession or control when it learned of the breach. With fungible goods, proving which sale replaced the broken contract can be hard, like a buyer proving which purchase was cover. Wisconsin Cranberry v. Groupe Alimonco (Wis. Ct. App. 2016): other sales weren't substitutes (different product, special contracts, much smaller load). Apex Oil v. Belcher (2d Cir. 1988): resale six weeks later unusable; delay unreasonable and seller had sold conforming oil the next day (cited only, n.15).

RULE Unfinished goods, § 2-704(2): seller may, in the exercise of reasonable commercial judgment to avoid loss and for effective realization, either complete manufacture and wholly identify the goods, or cease and resell for scrap or salvage, or proceed in any other reasonable manner. § 2-704(1)(b) lets it resell unfinished goods demonstrably intended for the contract.

Market — § 2-708(1)
RULE § 2-708(1): unpaid contract price − market price at the time and place for tender, + incidental damages, − expenses saved. Ignore the word "unpaid" for now: prepayments are handled separately (Section XXVII). The formulas are "strongly worded suggestions"; if one misses the expectancy, follow § 1-305.

- Seller's timing rule differs from the buyer's: time for tender, not when the party learned of the breach. The text asks why a seller treating repudiation as an immediate breach must wait for a later price.

- § 2-723(1) exception: if a repudiation case comes to trial before the time for performance, use the price when seller learned of the repudiation.

- Proof is hard for unique goods and easy for fungibles with published quotations (§ 2-724).

NOTE CASE Peace River Seed Coop. v. Proseeds Marketing (Or. 2014) — market damages after a resale Source: note case: the casebook quotes it in nn.17–18, p. 415. No class slides. Held: An aggrieved seller may claim § 2-708(1) market damages even if it resold and market damages exceed resale damages. A fixed-price contract allocates market risk, so market damages are what the parties bargained for. A seller isn't required to resell, so mitigation can't force it to use the resale price, and the UCC rejects election of remedies. Why it matters: Answers the question the text poses: resale and market are alternatives, but resale doesn't necessarily lock the seller into its resale price. Counterargument: § 1-305 forbids a recovery above the seller's real loss, and the resale shows that loss. A seller can avoid § 2-706 simply by not identifying the resale to the broken contract (n.19).

- Resale price vs. market price: the difference may reflect the passage of time (who bears that risk?) or the seller's negotiating skill. If seller recovers market damages and later resells higher, § 2-706(6) suggests no accounting.

Lost profit — § 2-708(2)
RULE § 2-708(2): if § 2-708(1) is inadequate to put seller in as good a position as performance, damages = the profit (including reasonable overhead) seller would have made, + incidental damages, + due allowance for costs reasonably incurred, and due credit for payments or proceeds of resale.

- Remedy of last resort, and implicitly available only if resale damages are also inadequate.

- Lost-volume seller: a jobber with unlimited supply is the clearest case; the breach costs it one sale, and any resale would have happened anyway.

NOTE CASE R.E. Davis Chem. Corp. v. Diasonics, Inc. (7th Cir. 1987) — who is a lost-volume seller Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, p. 418 (n.20). No class slides. Held: Capacity alone isn't enough. Ask not only whether seller could have produced the breached units on top of its actual volume, but whether it would have been profitable to do so. Under diminishing returns, at some volume the next sale stops being worthwhile, and awarding presumed lost profit would overcompensate. Why it matters: A manufacturer must show capacity and profitability. The usual test on an exam.

Lost-profit math (pp. 419–421) | Why
Profit = sale price − fixed costs − variable costs | Fixed = overhead (rent, CEO salary). Variable = rises with output (raw materials)
Statute adds overhead back: recovery = sale price − variable costs | Saves allocating overhead to one contract
Add unreimbursed reliance costs: recovery = sale price − variable costs + unreimbursed reliance | "Due allowance for costs reasonably incurred": money already spent that seller can't recover, because it gets only profit, not the price
Ignore "due credit for ... proceeds of resale" | Likely a drafting mistake. Applied literally it would almost always leave a lost-volume seller with nothing, contrary to § 1-305

- Wages and utilities can go either way: fixed if the sale was small against normal output; variable if it needed overtime. Tax treatment has little bearing.

- Direct, not consequential. A seller's lost profit comes from the breached contract itself, so foreseeability and mitigation limits generally don't apply (contrast a buyer's lost profits on resale, which are consequential).

- Lost profit is no ceiling. A buyer can't use a low or zero profit to cut market or resale damages: § 2-708(2) applies only when other measures are inadequate, not when they are higher (Trans World Metals v. Southwire (7th Cir. 1985), the leading case, n.26).

- Problem 9-8 (not assigned): lathe sold for $90,000; cost $80,000 + $2,000 parts + $1,500 preparation. Lost profit = $90,000 − $83,500 = $6,500 (the $500 overhead isn't deducted). Add unreimbursed reliance: $1,000 cancellation fee + $1,200 parts it can't reuse ($2,000 − $800) = $8,700. Market damages are zero ($90,000 market), and § 2-708(1) is inadequate if Sawtooth is lost-volume.

The price, when the seller keeps the goods

- Why the price? If seller truly can't resell, resale price is meaningless, market price may not be $0, and lost profit leaves seller stuck with its production costs. So § 2-709(1)(b) gives the contract price.

- Seller must hold the goods for buyer while suing. If resale becomes possible it may resell before collecting; net proceeds are credited. Payment of the judgment entitles buyer to any goods not resold (§ 2-709(2)).

- If seller is held not entitled to the price, it still gets § 2-708 damages (§ 2-709(3)).

NOTE CASE Foxco Indus. v. Fabric World, Inc. (5th Cir. 1979) — "unable to resell at a reasonable price" Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, pp. 423–424 (n.27). No class slides. Held: Seller of specially made spring fabric needed only reasonable efforts to resell at a reasonable price. The goods were made for a customer, were hard to sell after the spring season, and the market fell 50%. The jury could find seller acted reasonably even though it made little resale effort for months and sold part only the next season. Why it matters: Goods need not be worthless. The test is reasonable effort and a reasonable price, and market collapse and seasonality count.

Incidental damages, no consequential damages
RULE § 2-710: commercially reasonable charges, expenses, or commissions incurred in stopping delivery, in transporting and caring for the goods after breach, in connection with return or resale, or otherwise resulting from the breach. No consequential damages for sellers absent a provision: § 1-305(a), and most courts agree (Validsa v. PDVSA, n.28). So separating incidental from consequential matters. The nature of the loss counts, not its amount: incidental storage costs reached $293 million in Commonwealth Edison v. Allied Chem. (n.29).

XXVII. Prepaying Buyers, Casualty & Limitations — §§ 2-718(2)–(4), 2-709(1)(a), 2-510(3), 2-725 WEEK 11

RULE Restitution to a breaching buyer, § 2-718(2)–(3): when seller justifiably withholds delivery because of buyer's breach, buyer gets back any amount by which its payments exceed (a) enforceable liquidated damages (§ 2-718(1)); or (b) with no such term, 20% of the value of its total performance or $500, whichever is smaller. Buyer's right is offset to the extent seller establishes (a) a right to damages under other Article 2 provisions and (b) benefits buyer received. Payment in goods counts at its value or resale proceeds (§ 2-718(4)).

- It works as a type of statutory liquidated damages. Sellers may keep the statutory amount without proving harm, or prove larger damages and offset them.

- Example (Problem 9-12, not assigned): $90,000 lathe, $20,000 down; market $80,000 at tender. (A) Valid $10,000 LD: return $10,000. (B) No LD: the statutory retention is $500, the smaller of that and 20%, and seller may offset damages it proves (§ 2-718(3)), such as market damages ($90,000 − $80,000) or lost profit, plus incidental damages. Compare Neri v. Retail Marine with McCann v. McSorley (cited only).

XXVIII. Leases: Scope & Lease vs. Sale — §§ 2A-103, 1-203 WEEK 12

- Article 2A (1990) governs leases of goods and is modeled on Article 2, so the study question is where it differs, and why. The differences come from one fact: in a lease the lessor gets the goods back.

RULE Lease, § 2A-103(1)(j): a transfer of the right to possession and use of goods for a term in return for consideration. A sale, a retained security interest, and similar deals are not leases. A sale passes title (§ 2-106(1)); a lease transfers only limited rights, and the lessor keeps a residual interest.

Why the sale/lease line matters

Governing law | Article 2A | Articles 2 and 9

RULE § 1-203(a): lease or security interest is decided on the facts of each case. The real question: is there a reasonable chance the lessor gets the goods back while they still have meaningful economic value? Yes = lease. No = sale with a retained security interest.

RULE § 1-203(b) bright-line test: a transaction in lease form creates a security interest if the lessee's payment obligation is for the term and not terminable by the lessee, and (1) original term ≥ remaining economic life of the goods; (2) lessee is bound to renew for the remaining economic life or is bound to become owner; (3) lessee may renew for the remaining economic life for no or nominal additional consideration; or (4) lessee may become owner for no or nominal additional consideration. - § 1-203(d) nominal: consideration is nominal if it is less than the lessee's reasonably predictable cost of performing under the lease if the option isn't exercised. It is not nominal if the option price or rent is stated to be fair market value or rent determined when the option is performed.

- § 1-203(e): remaining economic life and predictable value are judged when the transaction is entered into.

XXIX. Finance Leases — §§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407 WEEK 12

- The idea: the lessee picks the goods from a supplier; a bank or other financer buys them (Article 2 applies to that purchase) and leases them to the lessee. RULE Finance lease, § 2A-103(1)(g): (i) lessor doesn't select, manufacture, or supply the goods; (ii) lessor acquires the goods or the right to them in connection with the lease; and (iii) one of: (A) lessee receives a copy of the supply contract before signing; (B) lessee's approval of the supply contract is a condition of the lease's effectiveness; (C) lessee receives, before signing, an accurate and complete statement of the supplier's promises, warranties, disclaimers, and remedy limits; or (D) in a non-consumer lease, lessor informs lessee in writing of the supplier's identity and of lessee's rights to the promises and warranties.

Buyer's remedy decision steps

- (1) Did seller breach? Is that excused? Are remedies limited? (2) Who has the goods? (3) Goods not delivered or repudiated: get them (§§ 2-502, 2-716), or cancel and take refund + cover or market + § 2-715. (4) Delivered: was it accepted? Check § 2-606. (5) Not accepted: was rejection rightful (§ 2-601 or § 2-612) and effective (§ 2-602; § 2-605)? Can seller cure (§ 2-508)? (6) Accepted: notice under § 2-607(3)(a), then § 2-714 and § 2-717, or revoke under § 2-608. (7) Add § 2-715, subtract expenses saved, and test against § 1-305.

Seller's remedy decision steps

- (1) Did buyer breach? Excused? Limited? (2) Buyer has the goods: price (§ 2-709), or reclamation (§§ 2-507, 2-702), or Article 9. (3) Seller or carrier has them: withhold or stop (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705); cancel. (4) Pick a measure: resale properly done? Market provable? Lost-volume with capacity and profitability? Can't resell? (5) Add § 2-710; never consequential. (6) Subtract expenses saved. (7) Account for prepayments under § 2-718(2)–(3).

Lease spot-check

- (1) Is it a true lease (§ 1-203)? (2) Is it a finance lease (§ 2A-103(1)(g))? (3) Consumer lease? (4) If finance and non-consumer: did lessee accept (§ 2A-407)? (5) Who bears risk (§ 2A-219)? (6) Apply the PV formulas, and watch which Article 2A difference the facts are built around.

TIP Traps to rehearse. Formula direction (cover − contract, contract − resale). A purchase that isn't a reasonable substitute isn't cover, so § 2-713 applies. § 2-607(3)(a) applies only to accepted goods. No "wrongful but effective" revocation exists. A seller gets no consequential damages. Nonpayment alone doesn't stop a parcel in transit. A retained-title clause is only a security interest. A $100 option on a non-terminable lease is a sale. A lessee's purchase can't serve as cover damages.
